topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - Nature
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on middle school education framework design; applicability depends on whether recommendations align with Australian curriculum standards and educational contexts.
takeaways: Embed AI competencies as part of a broader digital literacy curriculum rather than teaching AI in isolation — this holistic approach helps students understand AI's role within wider technology ecosystems.
Target middle school as a critical intervention point for foundational AI literacy before students specialise in secondary education, building conceptual understanding before technical skills.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on faculty development in public health education contexts. Findings may not generalise to other sectors or to non-academic workplace settings. Geographic scope unclear from title and snippet.
takeaways: Faculty resistance to AI adoption is often rooted in capability gaps rather than unwillingness; structured professional development programs can shift mindsets from resistance to readiness.
Public health educators need tailored AI literacy training that connects AI applications to domain-specific problems (e.g., epidemiology, health policy) rather than generic AI concepts.

Institutional investment in faculty upskilling is a prerequisite for embedding AI literacy into curricula — instructors must model comfort and competence with AI tools before expecting students to develop these capabilities.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health - Nature
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focused on European digital public health context. Framework may require adaptation for Australian healthcare settings, different regulatory environments, and funding structures.
takeaways: Use the identified competency framework as a reference point to audit current AI literacy gaps in your public health or digital health workforce, then prioritize which capabilities to build first based on organizational needs.
The European focus means frameworks addressing EU regulations (GDPR, AI Act) may not directly transfer to Australia — consult local compliance requirements before implementing competency standards.
Competency frameworks for digital public health can guide structured training design; identify which competencies exist in-house versus require external recruitment or upskilling programs.

articles.title: Upskilling and reskilling priorities for the gen AI era - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Upskilling and reskilling priorities for the gen AI era  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on McKinsey's consulting work across sectors, but findings reflect client organisations primarily in developed economies. Applicability to Australian small-to-medium enterprises or non-profit sectors may be limited.
takeaways: Identify which roles in your organisation will be augmented vs. displaced by gen AI, then prioritise upskilling pathways for those in augmented roles rather than attempting broad org-wide reskilling.

Combine technical AI literacy (prompt engineering, tool use) with domain expertise and soft skills (critical thinking, change management) — technical skills alone are insufficient for sustainable capability development.

Design phased upskilling interventions that start with high-impact use cases relevant to your business, rather than generic AI training, to drive adoption and demonstrate value to frontline employees.

articles.title: ASPIRE: a pedagogical framework for integrating generative artificial intelligence in public health education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: ASPIRE: a pedagogical framework for integrating generative artificial intelligence in public health education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — framework is designed specifically for public health education contexts; applicability to other sectors or disciplines is unclear without details on validation scope.
takeaways: The ASPIRE framework provides a structured pedagogical model for designing AI literacy programmes; identify which of its components (e.g. awareness, scaffolding, practice, reflection, evaluation) map to your organisation's current training gaps.

Public health educators can use this framework to sequence AI skill-building from foundational understanding through applied problem-solving; consider how to adapt these stages for your employee cohort's baseline knowledge and role-specific use cases.

articles.title: Development and influencing factors of artificial intelligence literacy and computational thinking in Chinese university students - Nature
articles.snippet: Development and influencing factors of artificial intelligence literacy and computational thinking in Chinese university students  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited to Chinese university context — findings reflect specific educational system, curriculum structures, and cultural factors in China that may not directly transfer to Australian higher education settings.
takeaways: Identify which demographic and educational factors (e.g. prior STEM experience, teaching methods, curriculum integration) most strongly predict AI literacy development in your student or employee cohort, then target interventions accordingly.

Consider how computational thinking foundations shape AI literacy outcomes — design upskilling programs that build conceptual problem-solving skills alongside technical AI knowledge rather than teaching tools in isolation.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability cannot be assessed without access to full methodology. The title suggests a dual-mechanism finding (positive and negative effects), but geographic scope, sample composition, sector focus, and study design are not evident from the snippet alone.
takeaways: AI adoption in organisations can simultaneously enhance and constrain employee creativity — understand both pathways (e.g., automation of routine work vs. deskilling or over-reliance on AI suggestions) to maximise creative output.

Design AI implementation strategies that explicitly protect creative problem-solving spaces; don't assume AI adoption automatically boosts innovation without considering how job redesign and employee autonomy are managed alongside the technology.

articles.title: Corporate sustainability and artificial intelligence-enabled workforce transformation: a dual-pathway model of employee capability, empowerment, anxiety, and job insecurity - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Corporate sustainability and artificial intelligence-enabled workforce transformation: a dual-pathway model of employee capability, empowerment, anxiety, and job insecurity  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — likely based on a single study with unspecified geographic scope and sector coverage. Findings may not generalise across different organisational contexts, cultures, or AI implementation stages.
takeaways: Design AI capability-building programs that explicitly address employee anxiety and job insecurity — treating these as distinct outcomes rather than inevitable side-effects of transformation.
Consider a dual-pathway approach: build technical AI competence *and* psychological empowerment (autonomy, voice, involvement in decisions) to sustain engagement during workforce transformation.
Measure both capability gains and psychological outcomes (anxiety, job security perceptions) as linked indicators of successful AI-enabled change, not just productivity metrics.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on the study's sample composition, which is not detailed in the snippet provided. The findings on the psychological mechanisms linking AI adoption to depression may vary significantly across different organisational contexts, industries, and cultural settings. Further examination of the methodology would be needed to assess applicability to Australian workplaces.
takeaways: Psychological safety is a critical mediator in how employees respond to AI adoption—organisations that fail to build trust and openness during AI implementation may inadvertently increase risk of employee depression and mental health challenges.

Ethical leadership directly influences whether AI adoption becomes a source of anxiety or engagement; leaders who transparently communicate AI's role, address fairness concerns, and demonstrate commitment to employee wellbeing can mitigate negative psychological outcomes.

When rolling out AI tools, audit your change management and leadership practices specifically for psychological safety gaps—lack of voice, fear of mistakes, or perceived unfairness in how AI affects roles are modifiable risk factors for employee mental health.

articles.title: Worried about AI in the workplace? You’re not alone - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: Worried about AI in the workplace? You’re not alone  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: US-focused perspective from the American Psychological Association; findings and recommendations may reflect US workplace contexts, employment law, and cultural attitudes toward AI adoption that differ from Australian organisational contexts.
takeaways: Employee anxiety about AI is widespread and legitimate — acknowledging these concerns rather than dismissing them is a prerequisite for effective change management and maintaining psychological safety during AI implementation.

Organisations should proactively address workforce concerns through transparent communication about how AI will be deployed, what roles may change, and what support (reskilling, redeployment pathways) will be available to employees.

Psychological readiness for AI adoption requires attention to both individual capability and organisational culture; line managers and HR teams need preparation to support employees through the transition, not just technical training.

articles.title: The mental health implications of artificial intelligence adoption: the crucial role of self-efficacy - Nature
articles.snippet: The mental health implications of artificial intelligence adoption: the crucial role of self-efficacy  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design and sample characteristics not evident from title and snippet alone. If based on limited geographic scope or sector, findings may not generalise across all Australian workplaces or industries adopting AI.
takeaways: Self-efficacy—employees' confidence in their ability to use AI tools effectively—is a critical psychological lever for protecting mental health during AI adoption; focus upskilling and training programmes on building confidence, not just technical competence.

Mental health risks during AI adoption may be preventable through targeted self-efficacy interventions; consider pre-deployment support (e.g. capability-building workshops, peer mentoring) rather than reactive mental health support after adoption anxiety emerges.
Screen for self-efficacy gaps early in AI rollout planning to identify employees at higher risk of mental health challenges and tailor support accordingly.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — without access to full methodology, generalisability cannot be assessed. Likely depends on sample size, organisational sectors included, and geographic scope, which are not evident from title and snippet alone.
takeaways: AI adoption can trigger distinct psychological responses in employees — some may approach new AI tools with engagement while others avoid them; understanding these contrasting motivations helps tailor change management strategies to different employee segments.

Job crafting behaviours (how employees shape their roles) may shift in response to AI; monitoring these shifts helps identify whether employees are proactively adapting or withdrawing, informing support needs during technological transitions.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI - Deloitte
articles.snippet: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Moderate — Deloitte practitioner perspective based on consulting experience, but lacks empirical validation or specific geographic scope; findings likely most applicable to large organizations with resources for formal change management programs.
takeaways: Shift from viewing AI adoption as a one-time technical implementation to an ongoing adaptation process focused on building sustained behavioral change in employees — this requires different change management strategies than traditional IT rollouts.

Design interventions that explicitly target the human behaviors needed for AI use (e.g., trust-building, comfort with ambiguity, collaborative work with AI systems) rather than assuming technical training alone will drive adoption.
Create feedback loops and iterative refinement cycles that allow employees to learn from early AI use and adapt their behaviors over time, rather than expecting full competency at launch.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet alone — geographic scope and sample characteristics not evident. Generalisability depends on whether study includes diverse sectors and countries; limited information available to assess.
takeaways: Employees' response to AI adoption follows approach-avoidance patterns — some actively reshape their roles to leverage AI (approach), while others minimise AI contact (avoidance). Managers should identify which pattern each employee exhibits and tailor support accordingly.

Job crafting during AI adoption is not passive acceptance or resistance, but active behaviour shaping. Create structured opportunities for employees to proactively modify their tasks and responsibilities as AI is introduced, rather than imposing AI integration top-down.

Understanding approach-avoidance tendencies helps predict how employees will adapt to AI tools. Screening for approach orientation early and pairing avoidance-oriented staff with peer champions or mentors can improve adoption outcomes and job satisfaction.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG analysis based on their consulting client base and industry trends, but findings reflect global AI adoption patterns. Applicable across sectors, though specific examples may skew toward large organisations BCG typically serves.
takeaways: Frame AI adoption as a workforce capability challenge, not just a technology deployment: prioritise reskilling and role redesign alongside systems implementation to reduce resistance and maximise change adoption.
Identify early-adopter roles and teams within your organisation to pilot AI workflows and generate internal case studies that build credibility and psychological safety for broader rollout.
Communicate the 'job transformation' narrative (roles evolving, not disappearing) explicitly and repeatedly—this addresses the core anxiety blocking behavioural change in many workforces.

articles.title: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — McKinsey insights are based on consulting engagements across multiple sectors and geographies, but findings reflect client organisations rather than representative sampling. Applicability varies by organisational maturity and sector.
takeaways: Frame AI upskilling as an organisational change initiative rather than a standalone training program—anchor it to business strategy, leadership alignment, and capability gaps to drive sustained adoption.

Design upskilling interventions that address psychological barriers to change (e.g. fear of displacement, skill anxiety) alongside technical content, using change management principles to increase employee engagement and retention.

Establish clear accountability structures and measure progress through behavioural and capability metrics—not just course completion—to ensure upskilling translates into actual AI use and value creation in roles.

articles.title: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be an editorial or opinion piece from a US-based business school without detailed empirical data or geographic specificity. Findings may reflect US labour market perspectives and may not fully apply to Australian workplace contexts.
takeaways: Identify specific AI-driven role changes in your organisation and create targeted upskilling pathways for affected teams, rather than assuming all roles will change uniformly.
Engage employees early in conversations about how AI will reshape their work to build psychological safety and reduce change resistance during organisational transitions.
Map which tasks in your workforce are augmentable (enhanced by AI) versus replaceable to inform realistic retention and reskilling strategies.

articles.title: The mental health implications of artificial intelligence adoption: the crucial role of self-efficacy - Nature
articles.snippet: The mental health implications of artificial intelligence adoption: the crucial role of self-efficacy  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability cannot be assessed from the snippet provided. The title suggests a focus on self-efficacy as a mediator of mental health outcomes during AI adoption, but sample size, geographic scope, sector coverage, and methodology are unknown.
takeaways: Build self-efficacy as a primary intervention target when rolling out AI tools — employees with stronger confidence in their ability to use and adapt to AI report better mental health outcomes during transition.

Screen for self-efficacy gaps early during AI adoption planning; low self-efficacy may be a warning sign for mental health difficulties and should trigger targeted upskilling or support, not just technical training.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: The science of why friendships keep us healthy - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: The science of why friendships keep us healthy  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: High — draws on well-established psychological research, though specific evidence base not detailed in snippet.
takeaways: Friendships aren't just emotionally satisfying—they have measurable physiological benefits, making social connection as important to health as exercise or sleep.
The quality and consistency of friendships matter more than quantity; one deeply supportive relationship can have stronger health effects than many superficial connections.
Social isolation carries health risks comparable to smoking or obesity, flipping the common assumption that health is purely about individual habits like diet and fitness.

articles.title: Your personality may be more genetic than scientists realized - Science Daily
articles.snippet: Your personality may be more genetic than scientists realized  Science Daily
articles.generalisability: Unable to assess from snippet alone — headline presents a claim about genetic influence on personality but lacks methodological detail, sample characteristics, or geographic scope.
takeaways: The counterintuitive finding challenges the long-held assumption that personality is primarily shaped by environment and experience — genes may play a larger role than personality psychology has traditionally credited.

This shifts the nature vs. nurture debate: if personality traits are more heritable than previously thought, it raises questions about how much individual effort or therapy can genuinely reshape core traits.

The discovery is noteworthy because it potentially reframes how we think about personality stability across the lifespan — if genetics dominate, personality might be more fixed than our self-help culture assumes.

articles.title: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe - University of Cambridge
articles.snippet: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe  University of Cambridge
articles.generalisability: High — the study examined musical preferences across multiple countries and cultures, suggesting findings likely apply broadly across diverse populations worldwide.
takeaways: Your taste in music reveals more about your personality than you might think — and these personality-music links hold up surprisingly consistently across different cultures and continents.

Despite huge cultural differences around the world, people with similar personalities gravitate toward similar music genres, suggesting some universal patterns in how humans connect emotion, identity, and sound.
The finding challenges the idea that music taste is purely culturally determined — it appears personality plays a powerful role in shaping what we listen to, regardless of where we're from.

articles.title: Out of the dark – Psychological perspectives on people's fascination with true crime - Perchtold‐Stefan - 2026 - Wiley & Sons
articles.snippet: Out of the dark – Psychological perspectives on people's fascination with true crime - Perchtold‐Stefan - 2026  Wiley & Sons
articles.generalisability: Limited specificity from title and snippet alone; likely reviews psychological research on true crime interest across populations, but geographic scope and whether findings are culturally bound remain unclear.
takeaways: People are drawn to true crime partly because it offers a safe way to experience danger and explore dark human psychology from behind a screen — satisfying morbid curiosity without real risk.

True crime consumption might tap into deeper psychological needs: understanding how bad things happen, testing our own survival instincts, or feeling reassured that 'bad people' are caught — it's not just entertainment, it's a form of psychological processing.

The genre's explosion in popularity reveals something surprising about human nature: we're simultaneously repelled and fascinated by real suffering, suggesting our brains are wired to learn from others' worst moments.

articles.title: How good is the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator for predicting leadership-related behaviors? - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How good is the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator for predicting leadership-related behaviors?  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — reviews existing literature on MBTI's predictive validity, but findings depend on the quality and diversity of studies reviewed; MBTI's scientific credibility remains contested across psychology.
takeaways: The Myers-Briggs Type Indicator has limited empirical support for predicting actual leadership behaviours — the gap between personality type categories and real-world performance is larger than popular business culture suggests.

Why it matters: millions of employees take MBTI assessments annually for leadership development and team-building, yet the tool's scientific foundation is shakier than most people realise — a humbling reminder that popular doesn't equal proven.

The 'type box' problem: MBTI forces people into discrete categories, but personality and leadership style exist on continua and change with context — a fundamental mismatch that explains why individual results often feel 'sort of right' but aren't reliably predictive.

articles.title: Which Personality Traits Are Most Important to Employers? - Association for Psychological Science – APS
articles.snippet: Which Personality Traits Are Most Important to Employers?  Association for Psychological Science – APS
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a summary or commentary piece without clear methodological detail on the underlying research scope or sample characteristics.
takeaways: Employers prioritize certain personality traits over others when hiring, suggesting that how you come across in interviews may matter as much as your skills.
The gap between which traits employers value and which traits actually predict job performance is often surprising — what hiring managers think they want isn't always what makes employees succeed.
Understanding employer preferences for personality traits could explain why some highly qualified candidates don't get hired, while others with different personality profiles do.

topics.label: Psychological Safety
topics.description: Research on psychological safety and its role in team learning, AI experimentation, and innovation.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample composition, which is not detailed in the snippet. The theoretical model linking AI adoption to employee depression through psychological safety and ethical leadership may apply broadly, but findings could be limited by sector, geography, or organisational context.
takeaways: AI adoption can harm employee wellbeing if it erodes psychological safety—prioritise transparent change management and create safe channels for employees to voice concerns about AI implementation without fear of repercussion.

Ethical leadership is a critical buffer against negative psychological effects of AI; leaders should model ethical AI use, acknowledge risks openly, and demonstrate commitment to employee welfare alongside technological change.

Monitor psychological safety and employee mental health metrics during and after AI rollouts; depression and psychological distress may signal that adoption strategy needs adjustment to better support affected staff.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG report likely draws on consulting experience across multiple sectors and geographies, but specific sample composition, methodology, and geographic scope are not detailed in the snippet provided.
takeaways: Create structures and norms that actively invite input from all team members, particularly those from underrepresented groups, to reduce barriers to speaking up and ensure diverse perspectives are heard.
Measure psychological safety outcomes alongside diversity metrics to identify whether inclusion initiatives are genuinely reducing status hierarchies and power imbalances in practice.
Model vulnerability and receptiveness to challenge as a leader — acknowledge mistakes and respond non-defensively to feedback to signal that the environment is genuinely safe for honest dialogue.

articles.title: Psychological safety in the changing workplace: Work in America 2024 - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: Psychological safety in the changing workplace: Work in America 2024  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: US-focused findings; while psychological safety principles are universal, specific workplace trends, labour statistics, and policy references are US-specific and may not directly transfer to Australian workplace contexts.
takeaways: Identify current barriers to psychological safety in your team (e.g. fear of speaking up, blame culture) using the APA's framework, then design targeted interventions such as normalising failure in innovation work or establishing clear 'no-blame' protocols for learning conversations.

Map how workplace changes (remote/hybrid work, AI adoption, restructuring) are affecting psychological safety in your organisation, and proactively rebuild trust through transparent communication and inclusive decision-making processes.
Use APA findings to build a business case for psychological safety investments with leaders—frame it as essential for retention, engagement, and innovation capacity in a competitive talent market.

articles.title: Superagency in the workplace: Empowering people to unlock AI’s full potential - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Superagency in the workplace: Empowering people to unlock AI’s full potential  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on McKinsey's consulting work across clients, likely skewed toward large enterprises and developed economies. Limited transparency on sample composition, sector mix, or methodological rigor.
takeaways: Frame AI adoption as expanding employee agency and control rather than automation or replacement; this framing reduces threat perception and builds psychological safety around upskilling.

Design AI implementation to preserve human decision-making authority and override capability; employees who retain meaningful control over AI outputs are more likely to experiment, take interpersonal risks, and voice concerns about AI failures.

Create structured feedback loops where frontline staff can safely report AI errors or limitations without fear of blame; this builds both psychological safety and organizational learning capacity around AI limitations.

articles.title: Debunking misconceptions about workplace psychological safety - Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health
articles.source: Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health
articles.snippet: Debunking misconceptions about workplace psychological safety  Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health
articles.generalisability: Moderate — draws on Harvard expertise but lacks detail on empirical scope; applicability depends on which misconceptions are addressed and whether recommendations are evidence-based or contextual to US healthcare/academic settings.
takeaways: Identify and challenge specific false beliefs your team holds about psychological safety (e.g., that it means avoiding accountability or that it requires consensus) to avoid implementing half-measures that undermine the genuine construct.

Clarify for stakeholders what psychological safety actually requires in your Australian context, since common misconceptions often lead to superficial 'niceness' initiatives that fail to create genuine voice and candour.

Use corrected definitions and examples when designing safety interventions, as misconceptions about what builds trust can result in wasted effort on activities that feel performative rather than structural.

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2026 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2026  PwC
articles.generalisability: Broad applicability across geographies and sectors, though PwC's respondent base typically skews toward professional services and larger organisations. Results reflect employee sentiment at a specific point in time and may not capture sector-specific nuances or smaller organisations.
takeaways: Identify which workforce fears (e.g., job security, AI displacement, work culture shifts) are most salient in your organisation by comparing PwC's global findings to your own employee pulse surveys — this reveals where psychological safety interventions are most needed.

Use the survey's global baseline on employee hopes and concerns to benchmark your current psychologically safe practices; if your workforce expresses fears that exceed global norms, this signals gaps in trust, transparency, or leadership communication worth addressing.

If the survey highlights anxiety about AI or technological change, proactively design safety conversations and upskilling initiatives that acknowledge these fears and position the organisation as a partner in managing change, rather than ignoring the concern.
